title: consumer
aim: Talk about consumer problems, marketing tricks, prices and things you do yourself.
objectives: Use clauses of purpose to explain why you do something
Compare products with comparative and superlative structures
Use have and get to talk about services

lessons.title: The customer is always right?

grammar.title: Clauses of purpose: to, so as to, in order to/that, so that
grammar.shortAr: للغرض: to / in order to / so as to + المصدر. مع فاعلين مختلفين: so that / in order that + فاعل + فعل. النفي: in order not to / so as not to.
points: Use to, in order to or so as to + infinitive to say why you do something; so as to is more formal.
Use so that / in order that + subject + verb when the two clauses have different subjects.
For negative purpose use in order not to / so as not to + infinitive, or a normal negative after so that.
table: Same subject
I often turn off my phone in order to avoid distractions.
Formal
The police put up barriers so as to stop people entering the building.
Different subjects
I’m going to send you all the information so that you can make a decision.
Negative
He set his alarm for 7 a.m. in order not to oversleep.
exceptions: With different subjects, use so that, not to/in order to: I sent it so that you could read it.

patient, pleasant
direct

grammar.title: Comparative and superlative structures
grammar.shortAr: المقارنة بـ than أو as + صفة + as، والمفاضلة بـ the + أعلى صفة. نستخدم much / by far للتأكيد، و the + المقارن twice لربط تغيّرين.
points: Use comparative adjectives for nouns and comparative adverbs for most verbs: busier than, more quietly.
Use (not) as + adjective/adverb + as to say things are (not) equal; use much, a bit, slightly or by far for the size of the difference.
Use the + comparative, the + comparative for parallel change, and ever with comparatives and superlatives.
table: Senses
It seems quieter here than I remember.
Equality
My chair isn’t as comfortable as yours.
Quantifier
This desk is slightly more expensive than that one, but it’s much better.
Parallel
The more you practise, the better you’ll become.
exceptions: Use ever, not before, with superlatives: this is the tallest ever.

grammar.title: How to summarise information from different sources
grammar.shortAr: للمصدر: According to... / From what he says... وللخلاصة: Long story short / All in all / In the end / It all comes down to...
points: Use From what X says / According to X to say where information came from; add a comma.
Sum up with Long story short, All in all, Taking everything into account or In the end.
Use Just because … it doesn’t mean (that) … and It all comes down to … to focus on one point.
table: Source
According to the reviews, the film is the best ever in the series.
Summing up
Long story short, no-one seems to agree which is better value for money.
Considering all
Taking everything into account, I’ve decided to stick with my current broadband supplier.
Key factor
It all comes down to the price.
exceptions: After question words use normal word order: It all comes down to when it would arrive.

lessons.title: I do it myself

grammar.title: Causative have and get; reflexive pronouns
grammar.shortAr: have/get + مفعول + التصريف الثالث: شخص آخر يؤدي الخدمة لك (have my hair cut). و get + شخص + to + مصدر: تطلب منه القيام بالعمل. و myself/yourself للتأكيد أنك فعلته وحدك.
points: have + object + past participle: someone else does the work for you, usually for payment.
get + object + past participle is more informal; get + somebody + to infinitive means you ask them and they do it.
Use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself…) to say you did something alone.
table: Causative have
I have my hair cut every six weeks.
Causative get
You need to get your eyesight checked.
Get somebody to do
I got a friend to take me to the airport.
Reflexive
Do you like this necklace? I made it myself.
exceptions: I have cut my hair = I did it myself; I have my hair cut = someone else does it.
